one_liner: Book sample timing std::vector<int>::reserve(n) before 100,000 push_back calls against the same loop without reserve.
what_it_does: A companion example (chapter03/03_reserve.cpp) for the Packt book Data Structures and Algorithms with the C++ STL. It times 100,000 push_back calls of an int into a fresh std::vector<int>, then repeats the loop on a second vector after reserve(100000), and prints both elapsed times; the neighbouring examples 01_sizevscapacity.cpp and 04_shrinktofit.cpp print how capacity grows and shrinks. There is no library to adopt: the takeaway is a one-line change, calling reserve(n) on the standard vector when the final element count is known before filling it.
how_it_is_fast: Without reserve, std::vector grows geometrically: each push_back that exceeds capacity allocates a larger buffer, relocates every element already stored and frees the old buffer, so 100,000 inserts pass through a chain of reallocations (about 17 if capacity doubles; the growth factor is implementation-defined). reserve(n) makes one allocation up front, so every push_back in the loop takes the in-capacity path: a capacity check, a store and a size increment. The technique is plain preallocation; nothing else is involved.
when_to_use: Filling a vector whose final size is known or cheaply bounded before the loop: transforming another container, decoding a record count read from a header, back_inserter output of known length.
Hot paths that build many medium or large vectors, where the reallocation chain (allocate, relocate all elements, free) shows up in a profile.
Element types that are expensive to move or copy, since every reallocation relocates everything stored so far.
Code that keeps pointers, references or iterators into the vector while filling it: after reserve(n), push_back does not reallocate until size exceeds n.
Latency-sensitive loops where one mid-loop spike (a large allocation plus a copy of all existing elements) is unacceptable.
when_not_to_use: The final count is unknown and the guess may be far too large: the excess capacity is held until destruction or shrink_to_fit, which is only a request (the repo's 04_shrinktofit.cpp demonstrates it).
Repeated small reserve calls in a loop, such as reserve(size() + 1): common implementations allocate exactly the requested capacity, which defeats geometric growth and can make n inserts quadratic.
A handful of elements: the single heap allocation still dominates, and a small-buffer vector that stores elements inline avoids the heap altogether.

Expecting the book's 3.2x in production: it comes from one run of a build that was most likely unoptimised; with optimisation the growth cost is a few bulk copies of the data and the gain can be smaller (not measured here).

integration.form: source-drop (one std::vector member call; nothing to install)
integration.min_toolchain: Any C++ standard library (std::vector::reserve is part of every standard); the sample uses a digit separator (100'000, C++14) and the repo's CMake sets CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 23
integration.thread_safety: Same as std::vector: reserve and push_back modify the container and need external synchronisation; the sample does not discuss threads
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the same std::vector type and API with one added reserve(n) call; you need n, or an upper bound, before filling

gotchas: reserve changes capacity, not size: elements must still be added with push_back or emplace_back, and indexing with operator[] up to n after reserve(n) is undefined behaviour; use resize or the count constructor when you want n elements in place.

Harness asymmetry: the reserve(100000) allocation sits before start2, so the with-reserve time excludes its one allocation while the no-reserve time includes all of its growth; the no-reserve loop also always runs first in a fresh process (the order is never swapped), so any first-use costs land on the baseline side. One run, no repetitions, no warm-up.

Neither vector is read after its timed loop and no optimisation barrier is used, so an optimising build is free to shrink the timed work; the repo's CMake defaults CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE to Debug and adds no -O flag, the likely build behind the book's roughly 120 ns and 37 ns per push_back.
Timing uses std::chrono::high_resolution_clock, which is not required to be a steady clock; steady_clock is the usual choice for intervals.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Use reserve first whenever you already have a std::vector and know the count: it costs one line and no dependency. The Qt 6 Cookbook raw-array sibling beats a vector filled without reserve, so apply reserve before concluding a raw array is needed; fast_vector still reports about 2x over std::vector when both reserve (12,991 ns vs 6,416 ns), and ankerl::svector or sfl::small_vector avoid the heap for small inline counts, so pick those when growth is not the bottleneck.
verified_claims_summary: The book reports one run of chapter03/03_reserve.cpp: 0.01195 s for 100,000 push_back calls into a std::vector<int> without reserve against 0.003685 s after reserve(100000), about 3.2x (derived from the relayed numbers). Compiler, standard library, flags and CPU are not stated, the repo holds no result files and its CMake defaults to an unoptimised Debug build; the numbers come from the book via the seed lead and appear on no repo page.
status_note: Stale Packt companion repo (15 commits, last on 2024-08-29 adding README errata; no issues filed) under MIT; there is nothing to vendor beyond the reserve call, which every standard library provides.
